title: Process State
body:
A [[Processes|process]] is not either "running" or "not running". It is in exactly one of
five states at any moment, and the [[PCB]] is where that state is recorded. Almost every
other note in the process group is really a note about one arrow in this diagram.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> New
    New --> Ready : admitted
    Ready --> Running : scheduler dispatch
    Running --> Ready : timer interrupt / preempted
    Running --> Waiting : I/O or wait for event
    Waiting --> Ready : I/O done / event signalled
    Running --> Terminated : exit
    Terminated --> [*]
```

## The five states

| State | What it means | Where the process is sitting |
|---|---|---|
| New | Being created; PCB allocated, not yet admitted | nowhere yet |
| Ready | Runnable, just not on a CPU right now | the [[Ready Queue]] |
| Running | Actually executing instructions on a [[CPU]] | on the CPU |
| Waiting | Blocked on something that has not happened yet | a [[Wait Queue]] |
| Terminated | Finished; PCB still around until the parent reaps it | nowhere |

**Only one process per CPU can be Running.** Ready and Waiting hold as many as you like,
which is why both of them are [[Queue|queues]] and Running is not.

## The transitions that matter

- **Ready → Running** is the only one the scheduler chooses. Everything else is forced on
  it. That decision is [[CPU Scheduling]], and [[Process Priority]] is the input to it.
- **Running → Ready** is a *preemption*: the process was fine, it just ran out of time
  slice or something more urgent showed up. It goes to the back of the ready queue and
  loses nothing.
- **Running → Waiting** is a *block*: the process asked for something (a disk read, a
  [[Semaphores|semaphore]] at 0, a keystroke) that is not available yet. See
  [[Waiting state]].
- **Waiting → Ready, not Waiting → Running.** This is the one people get wrong. When the
  [[Interrupts|interrupt]] says your disk read finished, you do not resume immediately;
  you become *eligible* to run and get queued behind whoever is already ready.

Every one of those arrows is a [[Context Switching|context switch]]: registers and program
counter out of the CPU into the PCB, next process's registers back in. That cost is why a
[[Spin Lock]] can beat blocking for short waits.

## Notice there is no "Ready → Waiting"

You cannot block on something without running first, because blocking is a thing the
process *does* (it executes a [[System Call]]). A process sitting in the ready queue is not
executing anything, so it cannot ask to be blocked.
